blocks.x: It's teaching school. It's going okay. I'll make a note that we're interviewing Mr. Henry Jackson, and the address is 3505 Magnolia. And let's see, this is August the 9th, isn't it? August the 9th. 1961. Right. Do you mind giving me your full name? Have any middle name? Henry Jackson. And can you tell us just what part of town you came from? Were you born right here in town?
I was born right here in New Orleans in uptown section.

This is what you call the garden district of New Orleans. What is your birth date? I was born in New England the 24th, 1909. And did any of your folks play music? No. Did your father or mother play any instrument or sing? No, just me.
I'm the only musician in my family.
No uncles or brothers? Anybody else that played any music? No, I'm the only one playing. Do you remember some of the earliest music you ever heard when you were a boy in the bands?

When I was a kid, I used to love to hear High Society play by Papa Salstein and Kiddo. I remember, and I remember riding a lot of times on the trucks with Jack Carey. He was one of the leading musicians in New Orleans at the time. I used to love to hear them play Chinatown. And I would get on the truck, ride. Do you remember who else was with Jack Carey? Chris Kelly was one of the musicians. And I had a drummer at the time. I don't know his real name, but they used to call him Johnny.
He's still around. He's still around.
He was a very wonderful little drummer at the time. And there's a lot of good musicians. I enjoyed the music. They was playing a lot of swinging jazz music, just like they do in the day.
And they were wonderful guys. Can you tell us how you happened to take up drums and when you took up drums? About how old you were? I'd taken up drums when I was about 20 years old.
I used to go around and listen to Buddy Pete Teeth and those guys in the Papa Salstein band. And I always loved to play the drum. I would get on tin cans and tubs, you know, and beat like that.
You started out beating on things.

I started beating on boxes with sticks. And I got my first set of drums when I was about 20 years old. And so from then on I started playing with different bands. Sidney Desvigny, they're one of the finest bands in the city. I stayed with that band three years.
Did you take any lessons from anybody or just pick it up yourself? Never to take lessons. Just play it for myself.
Play it. Started from scratch from the soup box and the tin can. And went on to the drums.
What kind of a drum set did you get when you were... Well, the first... When I first started, I bought a Ludwig set. A drum set from a pawn shop.
Yeah. And I went to a pawn shop and got my first set of drums. Ludwig. And I played those. You had cymbals in them. Yeah, cymbals. Any other tracks?
Like wood blocks? Tom-toms.
Wood blocks. Had the Chinese cymbals and the gun. I had all that. And I had the tum-toms. Big round tum-toms. I played those. Stayed around. Played those a long time.
Do you remember which pawn shop you got? Yeah.
I bought my first set of drums from the security lawn office. Oh, yeah. On Rampoche. New Canal. Yep. That's where I bought my first set of drums.
I don't think they have much in the way of instruments. They have a few trumpets, I think. They have a few trumpets there. So I bought my first set from those people, that company.
And I played a long time with them. Played in different clubs. Played around here at different little bars and things.
Yeah.
And played at different little picnics. I played a lot of picnics. And I finally joined up with Sidney Desvene Band.
How long had you played before you joined Sidney?
I had been playing, I'd say about 10 years. Between 10 and 15 years before I joined Sidney's band.
Who else was in his band when he...

Alvin Alcorn. We had Alvin Alcorn on trumpet. Had Sidney on trumpet. Joe Phillips was on trumpet. Louis Cottrell, the president, was playing tenor. Sam Lee, he was on tenor. And we had Jerry Green, he was playing bass. We had Oscar Ruzon. He was an alto man. And we had myself, I was on drums. And we had Buddy Charles, William Charles, he was playing guitar. And Raymond Anker was a singer and director of the band at the time. And they had a wonderful band.
And where did you all play in those days? We played different clubs.

Played all the Catholic schools. We played Xavier University. We played the prep. We played... We played... St. Catherine. That was a church auditorium. We played all the balls for the different clubs. The Illinois and our young men Illinois. And we played a lot of... A lot of different clubs around town. The Artaban Tea Room. Played that.
I remember when they used to play at the San Jacinto Hall sometimes.

Did you play some of those jobs too? Played a lot of dance at the San Jacinto and the old Gypsy Tea Room. Oh yeah. The old Gypsy Tea Room. We used to play there every weekend. And we played... There were a lot of those clubs around New Orleans. White and colored clubs.
Did he use mostly arrangements? Stock arrangements or special arrangements? What kind of music did you... They used...

They had a few stocks. Then they had Joe Phillip and Alvin Alcorn writing. Joe Phillip used to write for the band. And they used a lot of arrangement that Joe Phillip written for the band. We played those. Then we used a lot of stock. A lot of numbers like Anvil Coores and all. Yeah. The old number. And the band, they really had a wonderful band. I enjoyed the time I played in it. I enjoyed the stay I was in it. And Sidney, he's a wonderful guy to work for. A wonderful guy to play for.
He died about a year ago. In California. In California. Yeah.
In California.
I met him there two years ago. Did you ever play on the boat with him? I remember he told us he used to work on the boat. I never did. I never did work the boat.

When I joined the band, it was after they left the boat. Yeah. But I remember Pete Marville and P. Ron, they was on the boat. Yeah. They were wonderful musicians too. Yeah. But Sidney, when I joined Sidney's outfit, they had left the boat. I enjoyed it.

I enjoyed it. Um, can you tell me, did you ever learn to read by yourself? Or did you, when you joined his band, did they have the drum parts too? Of course, the drummer doesn't have to read as much music as the other people. I just wondered.

Well, at that time, I didn't have to read as much music because all they wanted to play. All I had to do was play. Push the band, you know. And the solos, I played the solos the way I felt. Yeah. I just wondered if they had any written drum parts. No. They had written drum parts, but they never did, they never had to read them. Never did have to read them. Never did have to read them. I just played like I felt. As long as you keep your ears open, I guess you. That's right. I kept my ears open and watched the band play. Yeah. Just swing the band. That's all I had to do. And I just pushed them. Push them.
And they loved it.

They enjoyed it. When it came time, the music had a solo in it. I'd taken the solo the way I felt. I took my expression. I played it the way I felt. And they enjoyed it. But I never did have to worry about reading anything in Sydney's band.
Do you still have the same set of drums in Sydney's band? No.

I don't have the set of drums. I have another set. I bought another set from Hall, about four years ago. About four or five years ago. From Hall Drum Shop. Oh. I got a wonderful set in there and I bought from Hall Drums. The drums. The drums I had Sydney. I just wore them at the time. I just wore them out. I just wore them out. I just made them warm up. You know.
Is that the same set you got from the pawn shop?

The set I was with Sydney was the one I got from the pawn shop. Yeah. Well, that's the wrong time. I wore them out. I wore them out. So I have another set I bought from Hall Drum Company. That's what I'm using now. Other than that, it's been a wonderful lifetime for me for music.
I was wondering, did you ever play any brass band? I never played any parades. Never played any parades? No parades.
I had a lot of opportunities too, but I never did like to walk. Yeah. I had a lot of opportunities to play parades. I always was a jazz musician.
Do you remember any of the parades when you were a boy and following what bands you heard?
I remember hearing Sam Morgan and the parade following those. Celestine, the original tuxedo band. They had marching band. The record band. The old re-record band when I was a kid I remember those.
Do you remember some of the drummers that were in those bands? Well, they had a drummer they used to call Benny.
I never really knew his real first name, but they used to call him Black Benny.
Yeah.
Louis Armstrong is also a lot of band. I must be the brand of his. He was a drummer. I remember him. Another.
What kind of drums did he play? He played a bass drum I understand. He played a bass drum in the parade, but he was a good trap drummer too. He played drums there.
For dances and all? Yeah, he played drums. He played drums outside of the parade. He played in small comedy, small band.
He played in small comedy. He played in small comedy.
He was the only one I can remember. Can you tell us anything about Chiney?
You say when you used to hear him and you?

Well, Chiney, he was a wonderful drummer. He was one of Celestine's original tuxedo drummers. He was a fine little drummer. He was the one who gave me my inspiration. I used to go watch him. I used to go to a club that used to call the Black Gold in a club that called Chiney Town where he would play on 7 and La Salle at the time. He was my inspiration. I used to watch him. He was a wonderful drummer. He could play. He was little and he sat behind those big drums and having those big 28-inch bass drum. He said you could hardly see him behind the bass drum, but you could hear him. I used to watch him and he was the one who got my inspiration to play. Watching him. I used to love to watch him play.
How big was your bass drum when you started at Ludwig that you got the long drum? That was 28-inch. 28-inch.
I went down to 26.
26 now.
26 now. Then another wonderful drummer used to play with Celestine. His name was Happy. I used to enjoy him. He was a good drummer too. Is that Red Happy?

Do you remember which Happy? Or is it Happy Gold? I think it's Happy Gold. The last one I was working on here at Paddock. Oh yeah. That's Happy Gold. He plays in Eureka. That's in Eureka. I played him and Henry Red Island.

That was my trumpet player. I used to love to hear him play trumpet. Him and Chris Kelly and Buddy P.T. Those who were trumpet players I used to get on the truck. When they would be playing on the truck I would hop on the truck and ride around. Listen to them. They didn't mind you getting on the truck? They didn't mind me getting on the truck because I used to be so little I could hand the handbills around. Oh yeah. They would get me all full of them. They'd tell me if you're going to ride you'd have to hand the handbills out. And I would hand the handbills out. And I would enjoy listening to them play. And they would stop at every corner. Every corner they'd stop I would hop off the truck and give the bills around. And they would be playing. And they would be playing. And I was like Chinatown, Tiger Rack. Those were his favorites. Yeah. And Muscat Rambo. I used to love them.
Do you remember who was with Buddy P.T. when you'd hear him? Who was in his band? Yeah. The drummer in particular? Who was you?

I don't remember who was in Buddy P.T.T. band. That was a long time ago. But he was playing here at the entertainers. That old club they called entertainers club down on Iberville Street. He was playing there.
But I don't remember who was in his band.
He only had about four or five men in the band at the time. Yeah. And I don't remember who was in his band.
I don't remember Chris Kelly's band. Who might have been with him when you heard him? The drummer or any of the other?
Chris Kelly's band, I think, I don't know who was in his band. That's been pretty long.
You say you have your own band now? You playing your own band now?
No, I don't have my own band now. I'm just playing with different bands now. Oh, I don't remember.
You have this picture up there you say was taken now? Yeah. In 50, 51. 1951.
This picture was taken in 51. This is Earl Bonham. This is a trumpet player, Garnier. Do you remember how his name is spelled?
What is it?
Garnier.
Garnier. Johnny Fernandez.
He's a piano player. They played piano. This fellow. And the trombonist. Were you there seventh All of the wonderful musicians are still playing.
Is that your new drum set now?
That is the drum set I'm using now.

The same one, the big, deep tom-tom. You notice much difference in the different size of bass drums, whether they're bigger or smaller, that make much difference in the tone? What do you think about it?
To me, the 26 bass drum is much better than the 28. And they have a 22, 20 inch, and 24 inch.

But those are really too small. Those are nice for combos, small combos playing in cabarets, you know, the cocktail lounge. But those 26 bass drums, what I like to play, I like to play. You got a lovely sound. You can hear it. I guess different drummers like different instruments playing. I like different sized bass drums.

Your old drum set, did you have cowbells too? Ever used those? I had cowbells, I got cowbells now. You still use them? Yeah, still use them. But you use them in a different way than you did at that time.
They had cowbells, the temple blocks on the top of the drum. Where are those temples? I use them.
You use them different now than you used to use them then? What was it different?

Yeah, well they're different in cowbells now. You use them more modernistic. Even when you're playing Dixieland, you don't beat them as much as you used to do. Sometimes guys just take two sticks, you know, just take two sticks and stay on a cowbell. Maybe all through a number, all through a curve. Get off one cowbell and on it to another. But now, he doesn't do that anymore. He might take and play a little rhythm, a Dixieland rhythm on one cowbell. And he might not use other cowbell all night. See, from that time he used both of them. But now, the average drummer you see now, whether he's playing Dixieland or modern drum, he ain't got, he don't have but one cowbell. You notice the drum was only one cowbell.
And how many did you used to have?
Oh, you had from three to four of them.
And it'd be tuned a little different?
Yeah, tuned a little different. See, and it was mounted on top of your drum.
Galbeth Jow has a scent like that. Yeah, yeah.
Yeah, yeah. One of the few that has them.
Did they used to sell those bells in the stores?
They used to sell them in the music store, yeah. Music store, you'd get them in the music store.
I don't remember seeing any lately.
No, don't see any lately, but you'd get them in the music store.
You don't know what company made them?
No, I never didn't know where company made them. I never didn't know where we made them. But you could get them in the store. I don't know.

Did you ever play in any smaller bands? I know you say you worked in a lot of different bands and all too. Aside from the bigger band, Sidney Desvinge's band, how many pieces was it? About ten or twelve or something? Sidney's band?
Yeah. Sidney had fifteen pieces. Fifteen piece.
Fifteen that band. I don't remember that band. You were a big band then, wasn't it? Fifteen piece band.

And I left them that, after the big band went out, they started hitting a lot of small combos. Well, that was from three to five pieces. Yeah. I played it from three to five pieces after I left Sidney's band. And that's about what I've been playing ever since I've been playing. Since I left the band, big band. I played a six piece band like this, five pieces, or a seven piece band. But most of the time it would be five musicians. Yeah. Most of the small bands are made up of five musicians.
Did Sidney get jobs always in that big band during the depression or were you with him during the depression? He got a lot of jobs.

But Sidney had more jobs than anybody else. He had the largest band around here and he was well known, well liked, and he was playing with the people like, so Sidney had more jobs than he could have at that time. Well, how much did they have to get for a date for one? Well, the most I got in Sidney's band for a night was four dollars. During the depression it was four dollars.
During the depression, that's what I wondered how people could afford to pay, you know. That's right. For such a big band of fifteen pieces would be. That's right.
During the depression, that was four, from three to four dollars.
Still for seventy-five or a dollars or so, I guess they could hire the band in for a night. That's right.
That's right.
But if it was a depression now, you couldn't hire bands for what they pay a band. No.
But at that time, and that was a lot of money to us.

Yeah, there ain't right. That was a lot of money to us. That was a lot of money. When Sidney would hand me that four dollars, that was a lot of money. And we played, we played hard, we played good, we enjoyed playing. It was a wonderful time, doing that, um, Sidney's band. Then we started with the small combos, I started playing the small combos, I've been with that ever since. I don't know when I would go back to a big band again unless it would be a boom. The only big band I see anything happening within the world today is bands like Count Basie, Duke Ellington.
Yeah, there aren't very many big bands. There aren't many big bands. There aren't many big bands.
But at that time you had a lot of big bands. Sunset Royal, Entertainment, Jimmy Lutzfoot, Andy Quick, all those of them coming. Yeah, there were a lot of big bands at that time.
Were there any other early drummers that you can remember when you were a boy?

Well, let's see, there was a, there was a fellow by the name of Roy, he used to play with Sam Morgan, Sam Morgan's band. I don't know if that is his last name, but he was a wonderful little drummer. His name was Roy, and he had one who used to play with Kid Rainey, his brother, his name was Rainey, but I never knew it was Joe Rainey. But when Joe Rainey was with his brother, he was another wonderful drummer.
It's not far from here, he's down on Jackson, he's a preacher now, works in the church. Yeah, Joe's the Witness.
Well, those two, Chani, I mentioned him, he was a wonderful little drummer.
Did Chani do any tricks with his sticks?
Yeah, he used to do, he would, he used to throw them up in the air. Oh yeah. Throw them up in the air and catch them, play them, twirl them on his fingers. He was a wonderful guy.

We talked to him a few months ago, he had one thing he puts on hitting the sticks together, sort of holding them up here and rolling them, you know, so one hand hits them in the other end. Did you ever see him do that in the old days?
I used to see him, yeah, I used to see him hold them in the trees and hit them on the sticks. Yeah, I used to watch him do that thing.
And did he have some way of singing with his snare drum?
Yeah, he used to hold the snare drum up to his mouth and sing to it.
Well, did he have his mouth against the head of the snare?
Against the head of the snare drum, right to his mouth when he would sing, and you could hear the vibration.
Right on the skin. Right on the skin.
And you could hear the vibration from the drum while he was singing. That was wonderful. I forgot about that. That was one of the things he used to hold the drum.
Was there any other drummers around here that you saw that had any tricks like that?
I didn't see anyone that had any tricks. Sidney Montague, he was a wonderful little drummer, but he never did do any tricks on the drum. He just always would play straight.
What about Black Benny? Did Black Benny have no tricks?

Well, Benny had tricks. Benny had a lot of tricks. He would throw the sticks up in the air. He would hold the drums in different kinds of ways while he was playing. He would hold the bass drum on the side and play, and the people would notice him. He would do a whole lot of other things with his bass drum. He would play in the parade. Yeah, the parade. He would take the drum off the strap and hold it down and play. Yeah, hold it in his head.
Yeah, hold it in his head.
He was a wonderful guy. Benny was. Yeah, he was a wonderful guy.

Did you say you never played any parades then at all? I never played on parades. Any other brass bands that you played, like any concert brass bands or anything else that you worked in? No, I never played on concert bands.
Just dance bands and theater. I played a lot of theater work during the time I had the stage shows at the Palace Theater. I played a lot of stage shows. You see, where was the palace?
The palace was at Dauphin and Iberville.
Oh yeah, sure, that's the one that was still there. Still there.
The lyric was up there as well. The lyric was up there as well. The lyric was up there as well. The next column.
That's where I was. The stage shows at the palace too. The palace too. But just before my time, the professor Robichaux was at the lyric.
The lyrics. The lyrics. Yeah, we heard about them.
Several people told us about that. Kid Punch and all of them. They were playing the lyrics at that time.
Did you ever play with Punch before? I never played with him.
And they had a drummer named Happy, too. He used to do a lot of tricks with the drummer. He used to play the bottles.
Bottles? Yeah, the bottles all strung up on the side of the drums.
And he played those bottles.
Which Happy was that? That's the one they call Red Happy?

Yeah, Red Happy. Well, he used to play the bottles. They had the bottles strung up on the side of the drums. And he could play a lot of drums. And he could play those bottles. I don't know how he'd do it. He'd put some of the bottles there and water in them. And something would be empty. Coca-Cola bottles. Old time pop bottles. I used to love to hear him play those bottles. Yeah, Red Happy. I used to love to hear.
That would make it sound something like those tune bells.
Yeah, that's right. They'd sound like those bells.
Did they put water or anything in them? Make them different hits?
Yeah, they put water in them. They put water. Fill something up with water. Something empty and something happy. Yeah. And had them tied with strings.
What did he hit them with? With sticks? With the rubber snare sticks. Yeah, regular snare sticks. Maybe he's like a triangle beater or something metal. I don't know.
But I think that was his own creation. I never saw that before. I'd never seen that before in my life. Then and afterwards. So that was his own creation.
Should the people see that all right? Yeah, the people could see the pits. They would shine the spotlight down.

Oh, down in the pit. They could still see them down in the pit. Let's see it. That was a wonderful thing to see. Yeah, it was that scene then. That was his own creation because I haven't seen it since and I haven't seen it after. I didn't see it before.
Were there any drummers that you ever got ideas from that you'd talk to even if you didn't take regular lessons that you'd go around and ask them anything or try to help you?

Well, I used to, they got, there was two of them I got inspiration from. There's two brothers, Paul Barbaran and Louis Barbaran. Well, those are my inspiration drummers later. They come later. Johnny come later. But they were wonderful drummers and they still are. Both still playing. Well, I got a lot of ideas, nice ideas from Louis Barbaran and Paul. Paul was playing with Louis Armstrong at the time. He came down here at this old Collier Center. Louis had a big band.
Fourteen pieces.

I remember I used to hear my parents too. Well, I used to go, I went in there and got a lot of inspiration from Paul. Paul talked to Paul and he told me to stick with it. And I, the father used to go around and listen to his brother play, Louis Barbaran. He's still playing now.
Yeah, he plays in South Central.

Yeah. South Central. I got a lot of inspiration from him. And my first one was from Johnny, from Aleta. When I really wanted to play and wanted to join those big bands, I got a lot of ideas from Louis Barbaran.

Are there any other bands you can think of that you played with? Any musicians in particular that you like that you worked with? Well... Especially the old timers. Yeah. We're trying to get into that old history as much as we can, of course. That's true.
Well, most of the old timers I played with when I was really young, one of them was a kind of player, by the name of Father Al, you heard of him?
Oh, yes.
Yeah. I played with him in a band during the time they had. And they were in a band.
You never did play with Jack Perry then, I guess. Before he died, I guess quite a long time ago. I don't know who to play with Jack Perry. I was too young at the time, one of them.
But I played once or twice with Buddy Petit's band. I sat in a band. And I worked in...
Did you ever play with Chris Kelly?
I never played with Chris Kelly. I used to go see him, listen to him. I never played in his band.
Who was your favorite trumpet player that you liked in those days? Did you like Buddy Petit or Chris or Sam Morgan? Or who would be your favorite?

Yeah, my favorite trumpet player at the time was Buddy Petit and Papa Celestine. Celestine. Yeah, Papa Celestine and Buddy Petit. And of course, all of them was good trumpet players. Chris Kelly, Sam Morgan and Kid Rene. Yeah. But those was my favorite.
Yeah, I heard Kid Rene and Celestine. I never did hear Buddy Petit before my time. Buddy Petit. He was a wonderful trumpet man.
And I was very young when I used to go hear him.
And do you notice any difference between the music then and now or the drumming then and now?

Well, I knew... The only difference I could see from then, from that time and now, is the music... The drums are a little more modernistic. In other words, look like they're beat more... More modern. But for a feeling... ...

Those drummers at that time, to me, they had more feeling than the drummers. You take the drummers at that time, they'd be playing, they'd be doing everything. They'd be making all kinds of motions. They'd be expressing their feelings. They'd be playing to show you what they're feeling. For the drummers nowadays, they look like they're playing more modernistic. They play more different from the guys who play that. I don't know, somehow they don't have much feelings as the guys are doing that. Of course, they play now. They play a lot of drums now. It looks to me that the drummers don't have the feelings that the drummers had in those days. Because those days, the drummer, if he knew something, he always did it. If he was throwing the sticks around, if he was hitting on the side of the bass drum, either the drummers would hit on the side of the drum stand. They'd make all those kind of things at that time. But now the drummers, he's got some modernistic now to let those things go by. They stick to their own set. They stick to their regular beat.
You think it's more like mechanical.
Yeah, that's right. But there are a lot of them playing now. They're playing a lot of drums.
Do you think that the music now is played faster than it was then? Or is there any difference in the time?
I think the music was played faster than it is now.
Yeah.

The reason why I say that is because numbers like Chinatown, Muscat Ramon, all those. And I'll be glad when you did, you're right. But they were playing those numbers up in tempo. But now the drummers, the band as a whole, they play in a modern tempo now. They play more softer, more sweeter. They play more in a medium tempo. But at that time, the band used to just let themselves go. I say, band, let themselves go and just play. Just play wild. Let everybody have a feeling. People be running all over the floor, doing a motion, stuff. But it looked like now, the band just calms down now and play medium tempo. Just once in a while, you might hear a band play up in tempo. But at that time, that's all you hear. Even the trumpet players, trombone players, they get on the end of those tailgates and just blow. Blow like they felt. And the tempo would be up in there. And while they was playing the two beat, so don't care how fast, you could never get away from the drummer. You know how fast you played it. So they was playing over a two beat tempo. But now the drummer's on a full, full kick. He is, just like I say, he's on a modern time. He's on a full, full kick. So in my time, when I was playing, when the bands that I played with, they would do a dance that they would call a linda hop. The younger generation would do a dance that they called a linda hop. Well, that was a fast dance where they would be hopping different steps on the floor. And up until now, if I play for a modern dance now, if I don't play a dixieland, I play for a modern dance now. I go to a modern dance. The dancers, the younger generation is doing something like a jitterbug. Something like a jitterbug now. And they're playing what you call a rock and roll music. A modern music. But they got some dixieland music. It can make you just as happy. Make you feel, when you're playing it now, make you just as happy. Make you feel less as good as if you was a dixieland. If you was a dixieland. They're playing some dixieland music now that'll sound like rock and roll. Actually, it's a fact. They used to take bands like the Duke of Dixieland. They play some dixieland music or rock. And what Louis Armstrong is playing now. A lot of music Armstrong is playing now. But he didn't play in his time. I heard him on Ed Sullivan's show a couple of times. He's a wonderful musician. A lot of music that he's playing now that he wasn't playing. That he's putting more than touch to it.
Do you remember any of the dancing in the old days? Did they have many waltzes or shodishes or other zerkas or anything in those days?

That's most about all I saw when I was a kid. When I was going to the matinee, was waltzes. The dancers, they called a foxtrot, a lot of rumbles. So they do a lot of rumbles. Now they do a cha-cha and all that. But they was doing a lot of rumbles, waltzes, a lot of two-steps. That's the dance you don't see anymore. Don't see that.

Do you remember any of the dances when they would have a march to start the dances with? Any of those? I don't know the name of the marches. Any clubs or any? I mean, do you remember? Did they always start a dance with a march? Some people told me a long time ago they'd have sort of a procession. They'd line up. Did you remember any of those?

I don't remember the marches. The dances like that? But when I was a kid, they used to have a march. They used to do that. They used to start a... Everybody would march around the floor. You couple... If you had a couple... If you didn't have a couple, you didn't march. But if you had a partner, you marched around the floor. That's when the dances would first start. That was the very beginning. I was doing... There used to be a lot of cocktail dances. The dances that would start at 3 o'clock. 3 to 5. For the younger people. And I used to do a lot of marches. I forget the name of the marches. I used to play. Some of the marches would be when the Saints go marching. Yeah. And they would play that. That's something you don't see now.
No. I just wondered. People told me they used to do that. I just wondered what the idea was. Was it to pick out your partner? You took the girl that you took to the dance at.

You picked out your girl before the dance started. You see, when they played the march, and you found your partner sitting down and marched when you had your girlfriend to dance. Yeah. That's the way that was. And so you pick... You walk around and pick out a young lady. And you all marched. Well, after the march was over, that was your partner.
Yeah.
That's it. I think that's what that accomplished. You picked out your girl and your march, and you had your day for the dance.
When you were with Sidney Desvene, did he play many of the carnival balls for any of the carnival clubs?
We played a lot of carnival balls. They played the young men of Illinois' balls. They played...
What was the young men of Illinois? Did that be like anybody that worked for Illinois Central or something? I wonder...
How'd they call it Illinois? Where'd that come from? Maybe they liked that name. She was up there. I didn't know. I wonder. Because it was from the north, I guess they liked that name.
Yeah.

But they never worked for no railroad. I wonder where that name came from. They never worked for no railroad. And Sidney played a lot of carnival balls. A lot of carnival balls. I didn't know who we were playing for, but it was carnival balls.
Would people be in costume or mask or anything?

Yeah, be in costume or mask, and at 12 o'clock they would take off their mask. Yeah. That was a law. They'd be pretty gown. Some would be in devil suits. Some would be in all kinds of costume. Yeah. In masks. And you didn't know who they were until 12 o'clock. 12 o'clock comes and everybody was unmasked.
Which halls did you use? Did you play? Those were carnival balls mostly. Did they have their own club rooms?

No. We played the Santa Simons Hall. We played St. Catherine Hall, carnival ball. We played the old Saint Sue Hall. You might have heard of that. Oh, yeah. I guess they tore that down. They tore that down. We played a lot of balls there. And they played most of them at the Santa Simons Club and St. Catherine. And played a few at the Gypsy Tea Room. Yeah. You might have heard of the Gypsy Tea Room.
Yeah. They call that tip top for a bar. They call it the hi-hat.
The hi-hat. Then they renamed it again to the Eptide. Oh, is it Eptide now?
Eptide. Yeah. Eptide.
Yeah. We played a lot of balls there. Most of the balls we played at this old Santa Simons Club. They renamed it now.
What would you down come? They still use that for dancing now? I haven't noticed any signs out in front. I think they took the big dancing sign down.

Which club is that? The Santa Simons Club. Yeah, they still use it. They name it the 5-4 Club. 5-4 Club. And they reopened it Sunday night. Oh, really? Oh, they just reopened it. Yeah, they reopened it Sunday night.
I thought somebody told me they were having dancing there now again, but I didn't know.
They reopened it Sunday night with an out-of-town band and an out-of-town singer.
Oh, really? Out-of-town, huh?

Eta James. Yeah, Sunday night. Yeah. Why do you use an out-of-town? Well, to draw the people. Yeah, see? Is that right? See, when they open a new club like that, they use out-of-town attractions to draw the public. And after the people get to knowing it, well, they're using the local outfit.
Suppose the people think the out-of-town band's going to be better than the ones here?
No, it's not the question of it's better, but it's the question of you're not seeing them. Yeah, something new.

New attraction, yeah. Something new, that's the question. Because over the rest of the country, usually for the last 50 years, they always thought the New Orleans bands were up to bed. That's right. Funny they'd have to bring in a band, but like you say, something new. Something new, that's right. I was wondering again about the carnival balls that you played, say, with Sidney Desveen or any other group. Did they play any special music, any different numbers? Just like a regular dance, I mean, did they have any special songs? Did they ever put on some of the big carnival balls? I understand that the auditorium, they put on sort of a pageant, you know, like a play or something first. Did the colored clubs ever have anything like that that they put on a little show or something?

Yeah, they have one or two, and we play a different type of music, play something like soft, sweet music, you know, for those things. Like they would put on a little float show. If they wouldn't have that, they would have a fashion show or something like that. Yeah, I think we do that. Say, well, we play a lot of the sweet music, sweet numbers for the fashion shows, things like that. Well, after, maybe that might last about an hour. Or maybe an hour and a half. Well, after that, the band would go back to swimming, go back to playing all these swinging hot numbers and sweet tunes and waltzes. But doing those fashion shows and if they have a little float show or something like that, the clubs would have. Well, they're sitting there special arrangement of sweet music you play for that special occasion. Other than that, the band just jumps all night long and the people forget about those gowns. They forget about the evening gowns they're wearing and just dance. Just dance as if they were in a regular street club.

It was a really wonderful thing to see. I was wondering about the Sydney's group. Did they ever play some, just had arrangements like just the whole group get away from the arrangement entirely and just, could somebody request something that they didn't have the music for? Could the whole band, the big band play all right?

That's right, the whole band. Numbers like High Society, we had a number they called Backbeat Booger. We had another number they called Red. We had a lot of Booger Woogers that just played when somebody asked for it. They said, play me Booger Wooger. And the music was forgotten about that. And everybody could play. The whole band could get together on that too. The whole band could get together. We all could get together, swing that. And there'd be many times that X's would put the music up. And X's would close the book. Let's go to play those numbers. Those Booger Woogers and those jump numbers that we had. They had a lot of jump numbers. They were called playing by here. And Sydney's band was well organized. He could play all that stuff. Sydney had a lot of numbers that he could play. And they didn't even have to open the book. That's what I wonder if they had. Yeah, he had a lot of wonderful numbers that the band could play. They didn't even have to use the music at all. We played those. A lot of those numbers were sounding just so good or better than the music that was written by the numbers of the band.

I never did get to hear it. I might have heard the band once. Oh, 1942 or something. When I first was around here. But how did it compare? I mean, it might be difficult for you to judge yourself if you were playing in it. But how did it compare, say, with Count Basie or Lunsford or some of those other big bands? Did it seem as powerful and as big as... Well, at the time...

How did it compare, do you think? At the time, I think the band compared as powerful as Count Basie's band at the time because they had a lot of young musicians in it and a lot of good ones. And they could play. They could blow. And to me, the musician was just as good as any musician you could find anywhere in the world. Just as good as musicians you could find in Count Basie. Maybe Basie might have been playing a different type of music. Or might have been playing a little fast or something like that. But as far as the musicianship and the playing, Sidney had just as good as musicians you could find anywhere in the world. Sidney had musicians that could sit in anybody's band. That could leave Sidney's band and go to Count Basie. And I guess Basie had members of his band and leave his band and come to Sidney. That's how good the musicians were. So that's the only way I could compare them. You had just as good as musicians in Sidney's band as Count Basie had in his band. You had a lot of wonderful musicians that could blow you a lot of horn, play you a lot of music. And your dad had bands in Sidney's band that left here, was playing right here, and left here and wasn't joining Basie like Joe Newman. That's right, yeah. Joe Newman was a hometown boy, played around here with us. He left here and played some small bands around there. He left here and went to North State up there with me. I guess if he had been a piece of so long, he wouldn't know how to play with all the bands. Yeah.
See, Earl Bostic, the saxophonist, did he ever play with you or with Sidney Diasbeen or other groups? I know he was here for a while.

Basie played here, but Basie didn't play with Sidney. But when he played with Sidney, I wasn't in the band. Tip된 stuff there with된 stuff there with된 stuff there with된 stuff there with된 stuff there with된

But he was a wonderful musician, the best he got. Well he's a hometown boy, was born and raised here. He left here and went up, been on his own ever since. He had his own band. Bosky is a New Orleans musician. Just like I say, he could play just as good or better as a musician anywhere in the world. And he improved himself. He's a wonderful musician, Bosky.
I was gonna ask about Sidney Desvene himself.

Did he play with the band usually? Yeah, he stuck with the band from the time he organized to the time the band broke up. He always was with the band. He had four trumpets and he was one of them. He'd sit right with them. He didn't stand up in front of them. No, he never just stand up. Joe Phillip and Alvin Alcorn would do the standing. Those were solo men. Alvin Alcorn, he played out there with Kid Ur.
Yeah, I know him very well.

And he's playing here now with Papa Salastain's band. Well, Alvin Alcorn and Herman Franklin and Joe Phillip was the featured men. Sidney just played his horn. He sat there and played. He never did stand up. He sat there and played. He could read. He could read anything you put for him. He sat there and played. When he got time for the solo, either Alvin Alcorn or Joe Phillip would stand up.
Sidney never did take solo? Never did take solo. Never did solo, but he could play. How was his tone? Was it very powerful?
He had a powerful tone. You could hear him. He had good lips for blowing. Wonderful lips for blowing.
Because I don't know if I ever heard him play or not. I'm not sure I did. I talked to him in California, but never did. He had wonderful lips. I don't remember for sure if I heard that band.
He had wonderful lips for blowing. He could blow. He could blow. And you could hear him. And he sat right there and blow for you. He didn't take his horn and sit in his lap or hold it. He played.
Yeah.

But for solo, sitting there with his arm, solo. Did you ever hear the P-Rone band? I heard the P-Rone band once or twice. They was playing on a roof garden here. Oh, up there on the Gravier about? Yeah, Gravier. That was his favorite spot. He had that spot sold up. And whenever it would be a dance up at the roof garden, it would be P-Rone. Remember who was the drummer? I don't know who was the drummer for P-Rone at that time.
There was one man, you know, Louis Cartrell's father, the old man Cartrell, Louis Cartrell. They played with P-Rone a long time. I just wondered if you remembered hearing him. I don't know.
I don't know. He had no man. But I'm going to see.
What did the band sound like? What's the type of band?

P-Rone had more of a concert band. His band was more of a soft music style. Like you hear those guys say, Guy Lombard, the Swedish music this side ever. P-Rone had one of the bands with the Swedish music this side ever. He had one of the bands with the Swedish music this side ever. P-Rone had one of the bands with the Swedish music. He was a violin player. Yes, I never got to hear him. I never got to meet him. He was one of the little cripple fellow, one of the little violin players. His band never was no hot band or no soul, but it was a sweet musical band. He played a lot of sweet music. He played a lot of sweet music, concert music. How big a band was it? Remember, there wasn't as big as Sidney's. It wasn't as big as Sidney's. It wasn't as big as Sidney's. He had about twelve pieces. It was a pretty big band. Yeah, a pretty big band. He had about twelve pieces. At that time, the big band was on the raise at the time. stuff like Walter Barnes, like Walter Barnes, where Walter Barnes got killed in a fire.
The band got된 stuff like

It wasn't as big as Sidney. He had about 12 pieces. He did a pretty big band. He had about 12 pieces. At that time the big band was on the raise. A lot of big bands like Walter Barnes. Walter Barnes got killed in a fire.
I remember reading about that.
This little saxophone player used to be in his band. At that time. Earl Barnes. He was in the band. Was he killed in this? No, he left. The band left without him.
The other band? No. The other band was from Chicago.

Yeah, Paul. This Barnes, they missed him one night. Somewhere he went out and the band went off without him. Intended to send for him. He was going to meet the band after leaving that. But before he could get to the band, the band would burn out. Yeah, it was terrible.

I'm going to ask a little bit more about Celestan too. How did he play? I heard him in the late years, right before he died. He had a small band. In the old days, did he have a bigger band? Was that a sweet band too? Or what was it like?

In the old days, he had a swingin' jazz band. Papa Celestan always did have a swingin' jazz band. No, he didn't. He had a trumpet player by the name of Guy Kelly. He was playing in the band. Louis Barbaran was playing with his drummer, a feature drummer. Yeah. And Papa Celestan had one of the best swingin' bands in the South at that time. His band always was with swing. He had a lot of swing music. When Celestan played soft music or concert music, it's only when you request it. But he had some powerful men in his band. Kimball, you might have heard of Kimball. He was playing banjo in the time. And he had this Russell, Bill Russell. And he had a... What did he play? He was playing trombone. He used to play down at the paddock. Bill Matthews. Bill Matthews. Bill Matthews. Bill Matthews. Well, that's Bill Matthews. It was a powerful horn man at that time. It was powerful. And Sidney had one of the best... Papa Celestan had one of the best swingin' bands you wanna hear. It was known as the original tuxedo band.

When he had people like Guy Kelly, somebody said he had shots with him for a while. How did he compare with the other trumpet? Was he as hot as the other fella or did he mostly take... Which one? Kelly? Yes. I mean, how was Papa Celestan? Did he see more people? Did he see more powerful than Guy Kelly? Oh. Or was Guy Kelly...

Well, Guy Kelly was a powerful man. Kelly was a solo man. Celestan played a lot of horn, but he wasn't as powerful as Kelly was. Kelly was a powerful man on the hand. People used to go to the dancers just to hear Kelly play. Yeah. He was standing on the back of those trucks and he was a powerful man. He had some powerful lungs for the blue. And he was much powerful than Celestan. They both were good trumpet players, but Kelly was more the powerful, more the better trumpet player. But they had a swinging band. They had one of the best swinging bands in the south at that particular time. They had this Kimball, he was playing banjo and guitar. He was a wonderful banjo player.
She didn't have her on piano in those days. They had Miss Kimball, Kimball's wife.

The same lady as the name of Jeanette Kimball. Jeanette Kimball. She was a wonderful piano player. She could play. She was playing. She played a lot of piano, still playing. That was his feature piano. He had Al of Alcon's on Alto. He's in Chicago now.
Oh yeah. That's Alvin's brother. I met him on that.
He was a wonderful alto player.
He played in Lee Collins.

He was a powerful alto player at that time. He could blow the roof off the house. And Lee Collins is another trumpet player from here. He's a wonderful trumpet player. He had his own group at that time. He had a small group. And South Stan had one of the best bands in the south at that time. It was swinging.
They always were swinging.
And there was a good drawing chord. Anytime they said Popper South Stan was playing somewhere, They didn't have to worry about the people turning out. You always draw a crowd.
How was the Sam Morgan band? Was that before South Stan was popular? Or were they both about the same?

They both about the same. Both were popular band. They were so popular they used to have Ballad of Music. South Stan was playing at the old San Suor. They used to have Ballad Foxes. They used to have boxes. See at that time you didn't clap for no band. You put the name on a band on a piece of paper and drop it in a box. See? Who run the battle? Yeah. Who run the battle? See when the people come in, South Stan's box be on this side, Sam Morgan's box be on this side. And you had a sheet of paper right there. You write which band you like and just put it in a box. See now you clap for a band. Yeah. You would go by applause. But at that time you put your name, see what was the popper you put your name on. Yeah. Who'd win those contacts? South Stan, Popper's original tuxedo band. You would have the most ballots in the box. I just wonder if anybody would steal a ballot of the box. Yeah. Who'd do it over with. It was a wonderful thing. Did you give them any prize or anything when it was over or just the honor of winning? It just was the honor of winning. I just wanted to know who was the most popular. Yeah. Sometimes the count would be close. Papas out there would always win. Anything else about the old time?

We don't have to fill up the rest of this tape if you can't think of anything else to tell us. I enjoy talking about it. Anything else about your life or any drumming or anything else you'd like to add before we quit?
The only thing, I went off with a few bands, played a lot of carnivals.
I wonder if you ever traveled with the ten shows and things like that.

Yeah. I went off with a world of moight, a cavalcade of amusement, stayed out there a lot of wonderful time out there with musicians that I didn't knew. When I got there, they had musicians there already but they needed a drummer.
There wouldn't be a band from here that would be made up here. How did the music compare away from here, some of those bands with the fellows from around here? Did they have as much swing to it?

Some of those bands, they had nice bands out there. They were nice swinging bands. But I don't know, none of those bands out there would swing like they were doing, like the musicians from the deep south. They would play, they would do wonderful music, but they didn't have the feeling the musicians from New Orleans had. Or from Baton Rouge or from down here. They just didn't have the feeling. But they played, they were good musicians playing. But it looked like all of New Orleans musicians, the musicians close around New Orleans territory, had a better, greater feeling than a lot of guys you would meet on the road. They admire you. They'd say, man, you come from New Orleans? I said, yeah, I come from New Orleans. I like the way you play. I like your style. I like your feeling. But I run into a lot of good musicians out there. But all the musicians I've seen, I've played with out there, met out there. And it seems to me that none of them had the feeling a guy had from New Orleans. Like the guys just from this part of the country had more feelings towards music. Like the guy from here put his whole heart and soul in music.
You know, I was told to this, something that's a little bit better about the music here usually than other places. That's right. Did you ever make any records?
I didn't, I made one recording with a singer here.
I forgot the name of it. Just accompanying the singer.
Yeah, just accompanying the singer. Well, I think that probably covers most of your life.

And this is something else you want to add. If not, we'll just, I'd like to take your picture before we leave. If you don't mind. I don't mind. It's not very bright outside, but anyway we can take it. All right, thank you.
